```{r}
##Part A
# TODO: Create three vectors of equal length (5 students):
# name (character): "Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"
# age (numeric): 20, 21, 19, 22, 20
# passed (logical): TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE
# Create three vectors
name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

# TODO: Combine name, age, and passed into a data frame called students
# using data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)
# Print students
# Create students data frame
students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)

# Print students
print(students)

# TODO: Check the type of the "name" column using typeof(students$name)
# and class(students$name)
# Check the type and class
typeof(students$name)
class(students$name)

# TODO: Now create a SECOND data frame called courses directly, without
# separate vectors first, using data.frame() with these columns:
# course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103")
# units = c(3, 3, 2)
# instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")
# Create courses data frame
courses <- data.frame(
  course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103"),
  units = c(3, 3, 2),
  instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")
)

# Print courses
print(courses)

## Q#1
#The data.frame() function requires that every column have the length because each row is one complete observation or record. If the columns have lengths R may recycle the shorter values when the lengths match; otherwise R will give an error that the arguments imply different numbers of rows.
## Q#2
#A data frame is like a list because a data frame holds columns and each column is a vector. Each column can have a data type, such as character, numeric or logical. However all values, inside one column must share the data type because a vector holds only elements of the same basic type.


##Part B
# TODO: Access the "age" column of students three different ways:
# students$age
# students[["age"]]
# students["age"]  -- note: compare the output/class of this one to the others
# Access using $
students$age

# Access using double brackets
students[["age"]]

# Access using single brackets
students["age"]

# TODO: Access the entire 2nd row of students using students[2, ]
students[2, ]
# TODO: Access the value in row 3, column "name" using students[3, "name"]
students[3, "name"]
# TODO: Return only the rows of students where passed is TRUE
# Hint: students[students$passed == TRUE, ]
students[students$passed == TRUE, ]
# TODO: Return only the rows of students where passed is TRUE AND
# age is greater than 19. Use the & operator to combine both conditions.
students[students$passed == TRUE & students$age > 19, ]
## Q#3
#students$age and students[["age"]] return a vector while students["age"] returns a data frame containing the age column. This is similar, to lists because double brackets ([[]]) extract the element while single brackets ([]) return a list containing the selected element.
## Q#4
#The and operator checks two vectors one element at a time. It gives TRUE when both conditions are TRUE for the same student. If I use or (OR) it will give TRUE when least one condition is TRUE meaning students who passed or are older, than 19 will be included.


##Part C
# TODO: Use str() on students to see the structure and types of each column
str(students)
# TODO: Use dim(), nrow(), and ncol() on students to report its size
# Get rows and columns
dim(students)

# Get number of rows
nrow(students)

# Get number of columns
ncol(students)

# TODO: Use names() (or colnames()) to list the column names of students
names(students)

# Alternative
colnames(students)

# TODO: Use summary() on students to get summary statistics for each column
summary(students)

##Q#5
#The summary() function produces results depending on the data type. For the column (age) it displays the minimum first quartile, median, mean third quartile and maximum. For the column (passed) it counts how many values are TRUE and FALSE. For the character column (name) it displays the length and class information. A mean does not make sense for names because names are words, than numerical values that can be added and averaged.
## Q#6
#The str() function is really helpful when I want to figure out how a data frame is put together. It shows me how pieces of data there are, what the column names are and what kind of data each column holds. Meanwhile the summary() function is better when I want to look at numbers and get a quick idea of what the numbers in each column are, like.

##Part D
# TODO: Add a new column called year_level to students with values:
# 2, 3, 1, 4, 2  (one per student, in the same order as the rows)
students$year_level <- c(2, 3, 1, 4, 2)

# Display students
print(students)

# TODO: Remove the "passed" column from students by setting it to NULL
# students$passed <- NULL
students$passed <- NULL

# Display updated data frame
print(students)

# TODO: Sort students by age in ascending order using order()
students[order(students$age), ]
# TODO: Sort students by age in DESCENDING order
students[order(students$age, decreasing = TRUE), ]

## Q#7
#No I could no longer use students$passed == TRUE after removing the passed column because that column no longer exists in the data frame. R would return NULL for students$passed so the filter would not work as intended. This shows why it is important to keep track of changes, in a data frame when performing operations.
## Q#8
#First the command order(students$age) tells us the order of the rows by looking at each student’s age and putting the age first then the next smallest and so on. Next students[order(students$age) ] takes that list of positions. Uses it to rearrange the rows in the data frame. The blank space after the comma means that every column, in the data frame should stay in the output. As a result the entire data frame is sorted by age and each student’s complete information stays together.

##Part E
grades <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"),
  midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70),
  final = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75)
)

# TODO: Add a new column "average" to grades that holds the mean of
# midterm and final for each student. Hint: (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2
# Calculate average
grades$average <- (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2

# Display grades
print(grades)

# TODO: Print only the rows of grades where remarks is "Failed",
# showing just the name and average columns.
# Hint: grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")]
# Create remarks column
grades$remarks <- ifelse(grades$average >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")

# Display only failed students
grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")]

## Q#9
#First I would create a column to calculate the difference between each student’s midterm and final grades. Then I would create another column to identify students with low midterm scores. I would sort the data frame based on these values. Compare them with the final remarks. By looking at the results I could identify whether students with grade drops or students, with low midterm scores are more likely to receive a failing remark.

##Conclusion
#A data frame is a two- structure in R. It holds information in rows and columns. Think of it like a table. Each column has a vector and all the vectors in a data frame must have the length. That means every column must have the number of entries. A data frame is similar to a list because it can contain vectors. But here’s the difference: each vector becomes a column.. Unlike a regular vector a data frame allows each column to have a different data type. You can have text in one column, numbers in another and logical values in a third. This makes data frames very flexible. They are one of the useful structures in R. Data frames make it easier to store real-world data. They help organize data. They make analyzing data simpler. Managing data becomes more straightforward, with data frames.

```
